title: Swole shaming is real, BIGot
summary: NH argues that 'swole shaming', ridicule of lifters, is real and widespread, especially in France, and comes from partners, other men, powerlifters, gym staff, teachers and mothers. He traces it to envy, rationalised jealousy, a mind-body split and a 'wimp culture' spread by Hollywood's jock-villain trope, and urges lifters to stay stoic, call themselves bodybuilders with pride and stay natural.
claims: Swole shaming, ridiculing people for lifting and wanting to be big, is real; he has dealt with it for 10 years and it can harm young lifters subconsciously
France has a big swole shaming problem; it mostly takes the form of constant micro-aggressions
Self-improvement is not narcissism; people who hate themselves project it onto others
Loving yourself is the key to happiness; only then can you be good to others
People resent self-improvement because it makes them accountable for their misery
Developing the body alongside the mind is essential; doing one without the other makes an incomplete human
He trains 2-3 hours a day, six days a week, while working 50-55 hours a week
People who say lifting wastes time usually spend that time on Netflix and the couch
Respond to passive-aggressive swole shamers by staying stoic, not returning negative energy
Partners often discourage lifting out of jealousy because you become more desirable; don't let a partner stop your self-improvement
Women are attracted to muscle in general, not necessarily shredded or steroid physiques
At parties he would play dumb with people who assumed a muscular guy was stupid, though he already had a master's degree
Swole shaming also comes from lifters, especially non-competing powerlifters insecure about their looks; the iron community should uplift each other
Calisthenics athletes, bodybuilders, strongmen and powerlifters all share the same love of iron and should respect each other
Gym staff have repeatedly told him he was intimidating, too heavy or too loud; commercial gyms are dying and you need a home gym
A philosophy teacher mocked him for developing his body when he started lifting
Swole shaming is driven by envy every time
Properly done, lifting lengthens life, keeps you mobile into old age, boosts hormones and confidence, and teaches that hard work pays
Men in Paris lose muscle mass every year; he used to be one of these wimps and grew out of it
Comfort-seeking, hardship-avoiding peers at his leftist first-degree college were visibly depressed and miserable
The jock-as-villain trope in Hollywood youth movies from the 80s spread the idea that athletic and big means bad
He was bullied extensively, even life-threateningly; it taught him that if you can't defend yourself physically you get crushed
The mind and body develop together; if one stalls, the other stalls. 'Educate the mind but make savage the body'
Envious people rationalise their feelings by declaring the envied thing bad, like students who call math stupid
If you want to find time to train you will; most people waste their lives
You can't claim bad genetics without having trained seriously for at least a year
At 15-16, before lifting, he had a wide waist, narrow wrists, very narrow shoulders and no muscle, the 'blackpill' picture, yet he got big by never giving up
Mothers often resist their child lifting because they don't want their baby to change; his mother claimed whey was steroids that would wreck his kidneys
Lifting is anti-fragile and anti-consumerist: lifters find contentment in training rather than buying things
Depressed men should start lifting before turning to drugs
The pain barrier stops people from lifting, but pushing past it is worth it 100 times over
Strength is anti-establishment: it teaches you that you don't need institutions to protect you
Call yourself a bodybuilder with pride for the next generation, despite the stigma
